description:
We are the Homeostasis Crew, and we’re here to set this challenge on fire!

Just like biological homeostasis maintains balance in extreme environments, we unite coding, engineering, medicine, environmental science, and the UN SDGs. From space healthcare to Earth observation, we build resilient solutions that matter.

Our Slogan: Keep up the pace, go up to space!
summary:
Our team created an online platform to track astronauts' health in real time. By connecting the spacecraft’s medical station directly to the ground medical team's computers, our system allows astronauts to do daily health check-ups and shows their health data across the mission timeline.
In space, noticing health problems early can save lives. Our platform solves this problem by showing sudden changes physiologically and psychologically right away. This helps the doctors on Earth act as early as possible before small issues get worse. We built this project using real medical advice from a doctor. It is currently a prototype, and we hope to develop it further to keep astronauts safe on future space missions.
details:
1. What does our project do and how does it work?

Homeostasis Crew is an interactive health-monitoring web platform that our team built specifically for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge ("Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions"). On long-duration missions where astronauts face space radiation, altered gravity, isolation, and closed environments, crews need a fast, reliable way to track their own health and spot changes early—especially when real-time communication with Earth isn't possible.

Our platform breaks health tracking down into structured, interactive modules and lets users observe and manage the system from three different roles (such as monitoring individual vitals, overseeing crew-wide status, and acting as ground or medical support). Users can input and track key health indicators like heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep hours, and mood. The interface uses color-coded status indicators, dynamic visual feedback, and clear explanations to help astronauts assess their condition at a glance and get immediate guidance on preventative actions or treatments.

2. What benefits does our project have?

  • Multilingual Support: Space crews are international. Including multilingual support ensures astronauts from different countries and space agencies can read health metrics, warnings, and medical instructions clearly in their own language without risking misinterpretation during high-stress situations.
  • Three-Role Perspective: Being able to view the system from three distinct roles bridges the gap between personal self-checks, onboard crew awareness, and flight surgeon oversight.
  • Instant Visual Clarity: Color-coded alerts and interactive breakdowns make complex physiological data easy to read quickly—no medical degree required to spot when a metric is drifting out of safe range.
  • Lightweight & Browser-Based: It runs smoothly in any browser with zero heavy installation, making it reliable for onboard spacecraft terminals, tablets, or habitat workstations.

3. What is the intended impact of our project?

As missions push farther into deep space—like Artemis lunar operations and future trips to Mars—astronauts have to become much more self-reliant with their health. Our team's goal is to empower crews with an intuitive tool that turns raw health numbers into actionable guidance. By combining clear visual feedback, role-based monitoring, and multilingual accessibility, Homeostasis Crew helps reduce human error, supports early intervention against spaceflight health risks, and keeps international crews safer on long missions.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did our team use to develop our project?

  • Coding Languages: Our team built the application using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript to handle the modular layout, real-time state updates across the three roles, dynamic status indicators, and multilingual switching.
  • AI-Assisted Development: We used OpenAI Codex during development to help structure the logic for role switching, organize the health indicator components, and speed up debugging.
  • Deployment & Hosting: We hosted our live platform on Netlify, allowing fast deployment and instant testing across devices.
  • Reference Data & Hardware: We referenced NASA’s Human Research Program guidelines on the five hazards of human spaceflight to pick realistic health metrics and thresholds, and tested our interface across laptops and mobile screens to simulate spacecraft tablets and terminals.

5. How is our project creative?

Instead of building a standard medical spreadsheet or a single-view dashboard, our team designed Homeostasis Crew around three distinct observation roles paired with multilingual accessibility. This reflects how real space missions actually operate—where an astronaut checking their own vitals, a crew medical officer, and flight surgeons on Earth each look at the same health data with different priorities. Combined with clean visual cues and interactive parts, our platform turns self-monitoring into an engaging, straightforward routine rather than a chore.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  • Challenge Alignment & NASA Guidelines: Our team carefully mapped our features to the NASA Space Apps prompt—focusing on self-assessment, clear instructions for non-specialists, visual clarity, and real spaceflight hazards (like cardiovascular strain, sleep disruption, and isolation).
  • International Crew Accessibility: Knowing modern space missions involve multinational teams, we prioritized multilingual support so critical health warnings and instructions are universally understandable.
  • Clarity Under Pressure: In an isolated or high-stress environment, cluttered interfaces cause mistakes. We focused on clean layouts, intuitive navigation between parts, and at-a-glance color coding.
  • Scalability & Performance: Using clean frontend code and Netlify ensured our app loads fast and remains responsive even on constrained hardware.
